title: Packaging Chains as pyfunc Models and Securing Endpoint Access

concepts.heading: Custom pyfunc for pre- and post-processing
concepts.body: When a chain needs more than one model call, wrap it in a custom Python function model. Databricks lists the reasons: the model needs preprocessing before its predict function, the framework is not natively supported by MLflow, the raw output must be post-processed for the consumer, the model has per-request branching logic, or you deploy fully custom code. You subclass `mlflow.pyfunc.PythonModel` and write two functions. `load_context` holds anything loaded once, such as weights or a tokenizer, so inference stays fast. `predict` holds everything that runs on every request: clean the input, call the model, turn logits into a label and a confidence string. Logging the class produces one artifact and one endpoint that contains the whole chain, so clients do not repeat cleaning or formatting code. One packaging detail: Databricks Runtime ML ships `mlflow-skinny`, but Model Serving needs `mlflow`, so name `mlflow` in `pip_requirements` when you log. A natively supported flavor with no extra logic does not need the wrapper.

concepts.heading: Files and parameters that travel with the model
concepts.body: A serving endpoint runs in its own container, so the notebook's disk and your volume paths are not there. Model Serving requires files from Unity Catalog volumes to be packaged into the model artifact: pass the `artifacts` dictionary to `log_model`, mapping a name to a path, and read the path from `context.artifacts` inside `load_context`. Shared helper modules travel with `code_path`. Real-time workloads perform best when dependencies are captured at logging time, so downloading files at startup is the pattern to avoid. Values that change between environments, such as the chat endpoint name, retriever settings or prompt text, belong in `ModelConfig`: key-value parameters taken from a Python dictionary during development or from a `.yaml` file for production and CI/CD. The agent code reads them with `model_config.get(...)`, and you pass the `model_config` parameter to `log_model` so the logged agent loads that set. The code file stays identical in development, staging and production, and the logged model records the parameters it was built with.

concepts.heading: Controlling access to and from serving endpoints
concepts.body: Two directions matter. Who may call the endpoint is set by its ACL: CAN VIEW gets and lists it, CAN QUERY adds querying, and CAN MANAGE adds updating the configuration, deleting it and changing permissions. An app or service principal that only sends requests gets CAN QUERY. What the deployed chain may reach is set by authentication. Automatic authentication passthrough is the recommended method when every resource supports it. You declare resources (AI Search index, Unity Catalog function, chat model endpoint, SQL warehouse, Genie Agent) when logging. At deployment Databricks verifies that the endpoint creator can use each one, creates a service principal for the model version, grants it access and injects short-lived credentials that it rotates. So the creator needs, for example, `Can Use` on an index, `EXECUTE` on a function, `Can Query` on an endpoint, `Can Run` on a Genie Agent or `Use Endpoint` on a warehouse, plus `USE CATALOG` and `USE SCHEMA` on the parents of Unity Catalog resources. Manual authentication means long-lived credentials you rotate yourself.

concepts.heading: Simple chains (generic LangChain pattern)
concepts.body: This part is generic LangChain expression language (LCEL) behavior, not a Databricks feature. A chain is a fixed sequence chosen by the developer: retriever, prompt template, chat model, output parser, written `retriever | prompt | model | parser`. Each component consumes the previous output, and the first component defines the input contract. A template with `{context}` and `{question}` needs a mapping with exactly those keys, so a request that sends `query` fails while the prompt renders, before the model is called. Repair it with a mapping step in front of the prompt, for example a dictionary of runnables that fills `context` from the retriever and `question` from the incoming field. The last step is an output parser: to return JSON the prompt states the keys and the parser validates them. Use a chain when the path never depends on a model decision, such as a fixed lookup followed by an answer. An agent lets the model choose tools, which adds model calls, variance and evaluation effort.

examPoints: A question about cleaning input, turning logits into a label, per-request branching or an unsupported framework behind one endpoint is testing a custom `pyfunc` model with `load_context` and `predict`.

A question about weights or templates that must exist on the endpoint, or about changing only the endpoint name or prompt between environments, is testing `artifacts` with `context.artifacts` or `ModelConfig` passed as `model_config`.

A question about who may query an endpoint points to CAN QUERY; a question about deployment failing for the creator or about short-lived rotated credentials points to resources declared at logging and automatic authentication passthrough.

quiz.q: A text classifier needs cleaned, tokenized input and must return a label with a confidence string instead of raw logits, all behind one endpoint. Its weights and a tokenizer folder sit in a Unity Catalog volume. How should the team package it?
choices: Log the raw model alone, put the cleaning and formatting code in every client application, and point those clients at the one endpoint
Subclass `PythonModel`, pass volume paths in `artifacts`, load them in `load_context`, and clean and format in `predict`
Keep the cleaning code in a Git repository and let the endpoint clone it and read the volume paths when the first request arrives
Log the raw model with a native flavor and mount the volume on the serving container so a script reformats each response afterwards
quiz.explain: One custom pyfunc model with `load_context` and `predict` gives a single self-contained endpoint, and `artifacts` packages the volume files into the model. Client-side logic drifts, runtime cloning adds a dependency the logged model does not capture, and a mounted volume is not part of the artifact.

quiz.q: A RAG agent is logged with an AI Search index and a Unity Catalog function declared as resources, then deployed with automatic authentication passthrough. Deployment fails for the data scientist who ran it. What explains the failure?
choices: The endpoint's own service principal lacks CAN MANAGE on the serving endpoint that Databricks created for the agent model version, so it cannot start
Passthrough cannot be combined with a Unity Catalog function, so the function must be called with a personal access token instead of declared resources
The agent must be deployed with manual authentication first, because passthrough only works after long-lived credentials exist
Databricks checks that the deployer can use each declared resource, and she lacks `EXECUTE` on the function or its parent usage rights
quiz.explain: With passthrough, Databricks first verifies that the endpoint creator can access each declared resource, then grants a created service principal access. A missing `EXECUTE`, `USE SCHEMA` or `USE CATALOG` for the creator blocks the deployment; the other statements invent requirements.

recap: Package multi-step chains as a custom pyfunc (`load_context` once, `predict` per request), ship files with `artifacts` and vary prompt or endpoint with `ModelConfig`. CAN QUERY is the least privilege for callers. Declare resources at logging so passthrough gives short-lived credentials, provided the creator can use them. Chains are fixed paths (generic LCEL); agents let the model choose.

title: Logging RAG Chains, Registering Them and Building AI Search Indexes

concepts.heading: Basic elements of a RAG application
concepts.body: A RAG application has a handful of parts to decide before logging: the model flavor, the chat model and embedding model it calls, the retriever, the package dependencies, an input example and a signature. Databricks recommends code-based logging (Models from Code): the chain or agent is a Python file that ends with `mlflow.models.set_model(chain)`, and `mlflow.langchain.log_model(lc_model="agent.py", ...)` stores that file. When the model is loaded or served, the file runs again to rebuild the chain, and a request calls `invoke`. Custom code takes the same route through `mlflow.pyfunc.log_model`. Pass `resources` so passthrough credentials can be provisioned for the index and endpoints. The signature, the input and output schema, lets AI Playground and the review app call the agent. For a `ResponsesAgent`, the interface Databricks recommends, MLflow infers a valid signature and you can skip the step. For a LangChain chain or generic pyfunc code you define a signature or pass an `input_example`, which must be a valid input to the model, and MLflow infers the signature from it.

concepts.heading: Registering in Unity Catalog and deploying
concepts.body: Registration puts the logged artifact under Unity Catalog governance. Use the registry URI `databricks-uc` and a three-level name `<catalog>.<schema>.<model>`; a one-part name fails. `log_model(..., registered_model_name=...)` logs and registers in one step, while a chain already logged in a run is registered later with `mlflow.register_model("runs:/<run_id>/chain", name)`, so the version that passed review is the one deployed. Each call adds a version. Creating a model needs `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA` and `CREATE MODEL`; adding a version to an existing model needs ownership or `CREATE MODEL VERSION`; loading needs `EXECUTE`. Aliases, not stages, mark which version serves. `agents.deploy(uc_model_name, version)` creates a serving endpoint with automatic scaling and credentials for the declared resources and connects tracing and the review app. Calling it again with the same model name adds the new version to the existing endpoint: traffic shifts when it is ready and the old version keeps serving. For new agents the docs now recommend the Agent Bricks CLI; Model Serving deployment is still documented.

concepts.heading: Creating an AI Search index
concepts.body: Databricks AI Search is the current name of Mosaic AI Vector Search; the exam guide may say Vector Search, the Python package is `databricks.ai_search` (older snippets use `databricks.vector_search`). There are three index shapes. A Delta Sync index with Databricks-computed embeddings takes a text column: `embedding_source_column` plus `embedding_model_endpoint_name`. A Delta Sync index with self-managed embeddings takes `embedding_vector_column`, an array of floats, and `embedding_dimension`. A Direct Vector Access index has no source table; the application writes vectors with `upsert` through the SDK or REST API. On a standard endpoint the Delta Sync source table needs change data feed (row tracking also provides it), and creating an index needs `CREATE TABLE` on the schema. `pipeline_type` is `TRIGGERED`, where you start each sync, or `CONTINUOUS`. All columns sync by default; `columns_to_sync` limits them, but the primary key and embedding column are always included. The index schema is fixed at creation, so new or changed source columns mean building a new index.

concepts.heading: Querying an index from a retriever
concepts.body: `index.similarity_search(...)` is the retriever's call. Plain `query_text` works only when Databricks computes the embeddings, because the index then knows the embedding model. With self-managed embeddings or a Direct Vector Access index, embed the question yourself with the same model and dimension that produced the stored vectors and pass `query_vector`; vectors from different models give meaningless distances. `num_results` sets how many chunks return, `columns` selects what comes back, and `filters` restrict results on indexed columns only, for example `{"region": "EMEA"}` on a standard endpoint. A column left out of `columns_to_sync` can be neither returned nor filtered. `query_type="hybrid"` adds keyword matching to vector search, which helps with identifiers. The caller needs `USE CATALOG` on the catalog, `USE SCHEMA` on the schema and `SELECT` on the index (the owner already has it), and with a Databricks-managed embedding model may also need permission on the embedding endpoint; production code should run as a service principal.

examPoints: A question about reloading a chain, serving it or letting tools call it without a signature is testing Models from Code (`set_model`), `resources`, and the rule that `ResponsesAgent` signatures are inferred while chains need a signature or `input_example`.

A question about a registration that fails or a version that cannot be added is testing the three-level name, `CREATE MODEL` on the schema versus `CREATE MODEL VERSION` on the model, and aliases instead of stages.

A question about `query_text` failing, a filter that returns nothing, or an index that must be created from a table is testing managed versus self-managed embeddings (`query_vector`), `columns_to_sync` and the fixed index schema.

quiz.q: A team built a Delta Sync index with self-managed embeddings stored in a vector column. Their retriever calls `similarity_search(query_text=question, num_results=5)` and fails. What is the correct fix?
choices: Embed the question with the model that produced the stored vectors and pass the result as `query_vector`
Change `pipeline_type` to `CONTINUOUS` so the index can compute embeddings for text queries on its own
Grant `CREATE TABLE` on the schema to the retriever so that it may run text queries against the index
Rebuild the index with `columns_to_sync` listing only the text column so the index knows which text to embed
quiz.explain: A self-managed index holds vectors only, so the query must be a vector made with the same embedding model. Sync mode, creation privileges and `columns_to_sync` do not tell the index how to embed text.

quiz.q: A RAG chain was logged in a run and passed manual review. The team wants that exact artifact in Unity Catalog as `prod.genai.support_rag` without logging it again, with the registry set to `databricks-uc`. Which approach works?
choices: Log it again with `registered_model_name="support_rag"` so the registry places it into the current default schema
Copy the artifact folder into the schema's managed storage location and let Unity Catalog discover the new model
Call `mlflow.register_model` with the run's `runs:/<run_id>/chain` URI and the three-level name
Create a workspace registry entry with the Production stage first and let Unity Catalog import its versions on a schedule
quiz.explain: `mlflow.register_model` accepts a model URI from an earlier run and creates a version under the three-level name, so what was reviewed is what is deployed. A short name fails in Unity Catalog, copying files does not register a model, and stages belong to the legacy workspace registry.

recap: Log RAG chains with Models from Code and `resources`; `ResponsesAgent` signatures are inferred, chains need a signature or `input_example`. Register with a three-level name and `CREATE MODEL`; versions need ownership or `CREATE MODEL VERSION`; use aliases. In AI Search, managed embeddings accept `query_text`, self-managed ones need `query_vector`, and only synced columns can filter.

title: Foundation Model APIs, AI Search Internals and Batch Inference with ai_query

concepts.heading: Serving an application that uses Foundation Model APIs
concepts.body: Foundation Model APIs expose Databricks-hosted foundation models as endpoints, so you build on them without deploying a model yourself. Pay-per-token endpoints are preconfigured, suit variable or intermittent usage and are the easy start; standard requests are best-effort, so latency can vary under load. Priority pay-per-token is opt-in per request with `service_tier` set to `"priority"`: it admits the request ahead of standard traffic, needs no commitment and costs a higher per-token rate. Provisioned throughput gives dedicated capacity for high throughput, performance guarantees or fine-tuned models, either on-demand with no term commitment or reserved for a fixed term and paid in full regardless of usage. AI Functions optimized models target batch inference. The thing you serve is the chain: log it with the chat endpoint and the index as `resources`, and passthrough gives the endpoint credentials. Querying uses an OpenAI-compatible API: use the OpenAI client (`databricks-openai` configures authorization), pass the endpoint name as `model`, and authenticate with a Databricks API token.

concepts.heading: How AI Search finds neighbors
concepts.body: AI Search has four parts. The source table (a Delta table, streaming table, materialized view or managed Iceberg table) holds the text or vectors. The index stores the embedded data with metadata and is a Unity Catalog object, so privileges apply. The endpoint is the compute that serves queries; one endpoint can host several indexes and scales with index size and concurrent requests. The embedding model, a Foundation Model APIs or custom serving endpoint, is used when Databricks computes the embeddings. Choose the index by who owns the vectors: a Delta Sync index follows a source table and updates incrementally, while a Direct Vector Access index suits an application that writes, updates and deletes vectors itself. Retrieval uses the HNSW algorithm for approximate nearest neighbor search and L2 distance; on normalized vectors the L2 ranking equals the cosine ranking, so normalize embeddings first if you want cosine behavior. Hybrid search combines vector search with BM25 keyword matching and merges the rankings with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, which helps with SKUs and other identifiers.

concepts.heading: Calling ai_query on table data
concepts.body: `ai_query(endpoint, request, ...)` applies a serving endpoint to table rows from SQL, notebooks or pipelines. The endpoint can be a Databricks foundation model endpoint, an external model endpoint or a custom model endpoint in the same workspace, and the definer needs `CAN QUERY` on it. What `request` may be depends on the endpoint: a `STRING` for foundation and external models, and for a custom model a single column or a `STRUCT` whose field names match the input features the endpoint expects. If the table column is `months` but the model expects `tenure`, write `named_struct('age', age, 'tenure', months)`. Optional arguments shape the result: `returnType`, `modelParameters`, `responseFormat` for chat models (plain text, a JSON object or a JSON schema) and `failOnError`; with `failOnError => false` the function returns a struct holding the response and an error message instead of failing the whole query. AI Functions are not available on Classic SQL warehouses. Run them on a serverless SQL warehouse, in a notebook or cluster with a supported runtime, in a Lakeflow pipeline or in a job.

concepts.heading: Batch inference as a pipeline
concepts.body: Batch inference means nobody waits for an individual answer: you apply a model to many rows and write the result to a table. For large jobs the docs advise submitting the full dataset in one query, because AI Functions manage parallelization, retries and scaling, and using Databricks-hosted foundation models (names prefixed `databricks-`) with `ai_query` instead of provisioned throughput, because those endpoints are fully managed and suit batch work. Pipelines combine ingestion, preprocessing, inference and post-processing and run as Lakeflow pipelines, scheduled jobs or Structured Streaming jobs. The incremental pattern: ingest new files into a streaming table with `read_files`, apply `ai_query` (with `responseFormat` to force a JSON schema), then validate in a downstream step with `EXPECT` constraints, for example a label that must belong to a list. Streaming-table ingestion is incremental, so files already loaded are not read again. Interactive chat is the opposite workload: it calls an endpoint per request and cares about latency.

examPoints: A question about inconsistent latency under load with per-token billing and no commitment points to priority pay-per-token (`service_tier`); guaranteed capacity or a fine-tuned model points to provisioned throughput.

A question about a service with no Delta table that writes and deletes vectors one by one points to a Direct Vector Access index; HNSW with L2 distance, and normalized vectors for cosine, describe how neighbors are found.

A question about scoring rows with a custom model points to `named_struct` field names matching the endpoint inputs; one about `ai_query` missing on a warehouse points to Classic SQL warehouses; incremental ticket classification points to a Lakeflow pipeline (streaming table with `read_files`, `ai_query`, then `EXPECT`).

quiz.q: A customer-facing assistant calls a pay-per-token chat model. Under peak load some answers arrive much later than others. The team wants steadier latency, still wants per-token billing and cannot sign a term commitment or reserve capacity. What fits?
choices: Reserve provisioned throughput for a fixed term so that the model has dedicated capacity at all times
Move the chat model to a Classic SQL warehouse and call it with `ai_query` so the warehouse absorbs peaks
Switch to an AI Functions optimized model, which is the mode meant for latency-sensitive interactive traffic
Send each request with `service_tier` set to `"priority"`, admitting it ahead of standard traffic
quiz.explain: Priority mode is opt-in per request, needs no commitment and is billed per token at a higher rate. Reserved capacity is a term commitment, AI Functions are not available on Classic SQL warehouses, and AI Functions optimized models are meant for batch inference.

quiz.q: A Databricks SQL job scores each row with a custom churn model served on an endpoint that expects inputs named `age` and `tenure`. The table has columns `age` and `months`. How should the job call `ai_query`?
choices: `ai_query('churn', age, months)`, because column order decides how fields reach the model
`ai_query('churn', named_struct('age', age, 'tenure', months))`, so the struct field names match the inputs
`ai_query('churn', concat(age, ',', months))`, because custom model endpoints only accept a single string request
`ai_query('churn', to_json(months), returnType => 'tenure')`, because returnType renames the input column
quiz.explain: For a custom model endpoint the request is a column or a `STRUCT` whose field names match the endpoint's input names. A plain string is for foundation and external models, and `returnType` describes the result, not the input.

recap: Pay-per-token for variable use, priority mode (`service_tier`) for steadier latency without commitment, provisioned throughput for dedicated capacity. AI Search: source table, Unity Catalog index, endpoint, embedding model; HNSW with L2. `ai_query` takes a STRING for foundation models and a matching STRUCT for custom ones, is absent on Classic warehouses, and incremental batch inference is a Lakeflow pipeline (streaming table, `ai_query`, `EXPECT`).

title: Sizing AI Search, Agent State Stores and CI/CD for GenAI Components

concepts.heading: Endpoint type and sync mode
concepts.body: Two choices set most of AI Search's behavior. The endpoint type: a standard endpoint gives lower query latency, supports Continuous and Triggered sync, both incremental, and high QPS scaling for sustained throughput. A storage-optimized endpoint offers a much larger capacity and faster indexing at a price tuned for very large vector counts, with slightly higher query latency; it supports only Triggered sync, and each sync partially rebuilds the index, reusing generated embeddings for unchanged rows. So billions of vectors rebuilt often with cost per vector as the priority point to storage-optimized, while a catalog of a few million vectors that must show changes within seconds needs a standard endpoint with Continuous sync. The sync mode: Continuous keeps the index within seconds of the source but provisions a streaming pipeline, so it costs more; Triggered runs when you start a sync with the SDK, REST API or UI and is the cheapest. Endpoints scale automatically with index size and concurrent requests, so you do not size clusters. The exam asks for the trade-off, not capacity figures.

concepts.heading: Controlling AI Search cost
concepts.body: AI Search bills for indexes, meaning stored vectors, and for endpoints, meaning query serving. Each endpoint has a base cost and one endpoint can serve many indexes, so eight small, low-traffic indexes on eight endpoints pay eight base costs. Hosting them together on a shared endpoint is the documented saving, applied when query volume across them is low. Triggered sync instead of Continuous, wherever second-level freshness is not required, removes the streaming pipeline. Endpoints whose indexes receive no queries still incur serving cost, so find them with audit logs and delete what is unused. A target QPS adds capacity that is charged whether or not traffic arrives, and high QPS is available on standard endpoints only. Track usage with the system billing tables and the built-in usage dashboards. Embeddings are a separate lever: an index can use one embedding endpoint for ingestion and another for queries, both serving the same embedding model, for example a high-throughput endpoint for ingestion and a low-latency one for queries, through the `model_endpoint_name_for_query` option.

concepts.heading: Persistent stores for agent state
concepts.body: Agent state comes in two kinds, and Databricks provides a managed store for each, both backed by Lakebase (managed Postgres) and usable from any framework. Agent sessions hold the state of one interaction, most often the ordered conversation history with tool calls and results, so an interaction survives a restart and can be rebuilt on a follow-up. Agent memory holds durable facts, preferences and decisions, recalled by semantic search in later, separate conversations. Memory is scoped to a subject, not an interaction, so deleting a session or a whole session store does not delete memory. A memory pipeline reads a session store, extracts durable facts and writes them to a memory store on demand or on a schedule, so memory builds without memory-writing tools in the agent. Use both stores together for most cases. For structured state that is updated and read within milliseconds, such as task status, Lakebase Postgres itself fits: a managed database for low-latency transactional work. Delta tables suit analytics, AI Search indexes suit retrieval. The earlier managed agent memory governed by Unity Catalog is Legacy.

concepts.heading: CI/CD for indexes and agent components
concepts.body: Databricks recommends the deploy-code pattern for MLOps: the code that trains a model or logs an agent moves from development to staging to production, tests run in each environment, and the production model is produced by a run in production. An environment usually corresponds to a catalog in Unity Catalog. In the alternative, deploy models, the artifact is built in development and promoted; when rebuilding is too costly, copy the tested version with `copy_model_version`, let privileges on both models decide who may promote, and move an alias, since stages are not supported. For GenAI the index belongs to the pipeline: a Triggered Delta Sync index does not refresh when its source table changes, so the job needs a task after the table refresh that calls `index.sync()` or the REST API. New or changed source columns need a new index. Testing agent components is generic practice on top of the documented pattern: unit-test tools and retrieval logic, run integration tests against real endpoints in staging, and evaluate on a fixed dataset before release. Calling `agents.deploy` again for the same model name updates the live endpoint without an outage.

examPoints: A question that pairs very large, frequently rebuilt indexes with cost per vector points to a storage-optimized endpoint; one that needs second-level freshness points to a standard endpoint with Continuous sync, because storage-optimized supports only Triggered.
A question about lowering AI Search cost points to sharing endpoints among small low-traffic indexes, Triggered over Continuous sync, and removing unused endpoints.

A question about resuming a conversation points to agent sessions, about remembering preferences later to agent memory, and about stale RAG answers after a nightly table refresh to a sync task; promoting without retraining points to `copy_model_version` plus an alias.

quiz.q: A catalog index of a few million vectors must show inventory changes within seconds. A teammate suggests a storage-optimized endpoint because it is cheaper per vector. What is the best advice?
choices: Use a storage-optimized endpoint with Continuous sync, since faster indexing makes up for its higher query latency
Use a storage-optimized endpoint and call the sync from a job every few seconds, which replaces Continuous sync
Use a standard endpoint with Continuous sync, since storage-optimized endpoints support only Triggered sync
Use a standard endpoint with Triggered sync, because Triggered mode also keeps the index within seconds of the source
quiz.explain: Continuous sync keeps the index within seconds but is available only on standard endpoints. Each storage-optimized sync partially rebuilds the index, and Triggered mode refreshes only when a sync is started.

quiz.q: A nightly job refreshes the source table of a Delta Sync index created in Triggered mode, but the RAG app keeps returning old content. What should the CI/CD job do?
choices: Add a task after the table refresh that starts an index sync through the SDK or REST API
Recreate the endpoint each night so that the index reloads the current source table when the endpoint starts
Enable `columns_to_sync` for all columns so that the index notices which rows changed in the table
Grant `SELECT` on the source table to the retriever so that queries read fresh rows straight from the Delta table
quiz.explain: A Triggered Delta Sync index updates only when a sync is started, so the pipeline must start it after the table refresh. A new endpoint, the column list or retriever privileges do not trigger a sync.

recap: Standard: low latency, Continuous or Triggered sync. Storage-optimized: very large, fast indexing, Triggered only. Cut cost with shared endpoints, Triggered sync and removing unused endpoints. Sessions keep one conversation, memory keeps durable facts, Lakebase serves transactional state. Deploy code through environments; sync Triggered indexes after table refresh; `copy_model_version` plus alias for promotion.

title: MCP Servers, Prompt Versioning and User-Facing Agent Interfaces

concepts.heading: Choosing and exposing MCP servers
concepts.body: Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the open standard through which an agent discovers and calls tools. Databricks offers three sources. Databricks-provided servers live in the `system.ai` schema; each is a Unity Catalog securable invoked through Unity Gateway (formerly AI Gateway), so grants control who may call it and policies control individual calls, and you host nothing. For business questions in natural language the docs recommend the Genie One MCP server (`system.ai.genie_one_mcp`), the only generally available one, because it grounds answers in the governed semantic layer instead of guessing from table names. External servers are self-hosted or third-party servers you register. Custom servers run on Databricks Apps. To expose an existing REST API with an OpenAPI 3 description, deploy the MCP Server (OpenAPI) template: put `spec.json` at the root of a Unity Catalog volume and store the backend credential in a Unity Catalog HTTP connection named in `UC_CONNECTION_NAME`. The agent connects to the app URL plus `/mcp`; callers need `CAN USE` on the app and `USE CONNECTION`. Other workspace MCP endpoints, such as a Genie Agent MCP, rely on permissions on the underlying resources without Unity Gateway governance.

concepts.heading: Prompt versioning as configuration
concepts.body: Prompt text changes more often than agent logic and can change behavior as much as a model swap, so treat it like code. This is generic practice built from Databricks pieces; MLflow Prompt Registry is Beta in the docs, so it is not taught as the answer. Keep the prompt in a file under Git, so each change is a commit in a pull request with an author and a message. Read it through `ModelConfig`, using a `.yaml` file for production, and pass `model_config` when you log the agent. The logged Unity Catalog model version then stores the exact prompt next to the code, which answers which agent version used which text. A registered version is a snapshot, so a prompt change becomes a new version and the earlier one stays available. Aliases, which are mutable named references, say which version serves. Logging traces with the model version lets you tie each answer to its prompt. Hard-coding long prompts in agent logic, or pasting them into an endpoint by hand, loses history, review and rollback.

concepts.heading: Prompt lifecycle: promote, evaluate, roll back
concepts.body: Prompt lifecycle follows the deploy-code pattern the docs recommend for MLOps: the same code and configuration move from development to staging to production, and each environment runs its own tests. A prompt edit is merged by pull request, a CI pipeline deploys that commit to staging and runs an evaluation, for example `mlflow.genai.evaluate()`, on a fixed dataset with the same scorers each time, and only a passing commit is deployed to production. The fixed dataset and scorers are what make two prompt versions comparable. The evaluation gate is a generic application of the documented pattern. Rollback is a deployment, not an edit: when version 12 lowers quality, deploy version 11 again, because its logged config holds the earlier prompt. Do not delete or rewrite the bad version; the evidence is needed to audit the incident and compare versions. Adding endpoint capacity helps latency and throttling, not answer wording, and editing a prompt directly in production skips both the tests and the history.

concepts.heading: User-facing interfaces for agents
concepts.body: Databricks Apps runs a web interface on the platform with no separate hosting: Python (Streamlit, Dash, Gradio) or Node.js, signing users in through the workspace and integrating with Unity Catalog and Model Serving. Agent chat templates such as `e2e-chatbot-app-next` stream responses, show tool calls and can keep history in Lakebase; that page is marked Legacy because new projects start from the Agent Bricks CLI, which also includes a chat UI. Slack or Teams bots call the same endpoint but live outside Databricks and need their own hosting and identity mapping (generic pattern). An app has two identities. App authorization uses its dedicated service principal, so every user shares its permissions and the app cannot enforce user-level rules. User authorization forwards the signed-in user's token, so Unity Catalog row filters and column masks apply to that person; the app declares scopes such as `sql` or `model-serving` that limit what it may do on the user's behalf. For least privilege, add the endpoint as an app resource with `CAN QUERY` and a secret resource, then reference both with `valueFrom` in `app.yaml`.

examPoints: A question about governed business metrics in natural language, with no server to host, points to the Genie One MCP server; one about an internal REST API with an OpenAPI description and a hidden credential points to the MCP Server (OpenAPI) template on Databricks Apps with a Unity Catalog HTTP connection.

A question about reviewing prompt edits and knowing which agent version used which prompt points to prompt text in Git read through `ModelConfig` and logged with the agent; the Beta Prompt Registry is not the answer.

A question about users seeing rows they are not allowed to read in an app points to user authorization with scopes, not the app's service principal; one about least privilege and secrets points to app resources with `CAN QUERY` and `valueFrom`.

quiz.q: A support agent keeps its system prompt as a string inside `agent.py`. Prompts change often, each change must be reviewed in a pull request, and the team must know which registered agent version used which prompt text. Which design fits best?
choices: Keep the prompt in a YAML file in Git, read it via `ModelConfig` and log it with the agent
Keep the prompt only in a notebook cell so that each analyst can edit the wording quickly and rerun the agent
Paste the current prompt into the serving endpoint settings after each deployment and keep older wording in a wiki page
Store the prompt in a Delta table that the agent reads on every request and overwrite the row when the wording changes
quiz.explain: A file in Git gives reviewed history, and logging `model_config` with the agent makes each registered version a snapshot of code plus prompt. Notebook cells, manual endpoint edits and overwritten rows lose review and traceability.

quiz.q: A chat app on Databricks Apps queries tables through an agent. It runs under its own service principal, so interns see rows that only a finance group may read. The company requires Unity Catalog permissions to apply to the person asking. What should the team change?
choices: Grant the app's service principal membership in the finance group so that it may read every row for all users
Create one Databricks Apps deployment per user and give each deployment its own personal access token for the agent
Add a row filter inside the agent prompt that asks the model not to reveal finance rows to non-finance users
Enable user authorization so the app calls Databricks with the user's token and declares the scopes it needs
quiz.explain: User authorization forwards the signed-in user's token, so Unity Catalog row filters and column masks apply to that person, within the declared scopes. App authorization gives everyone the service principal's access, and a prompt instruction is not an access control.

recap: Genie One is the GA Databricks-provided MCP server for governed business questions; `system.ai` servers are governed through Unity Gateway. Wrap a REST API with the OpenAPI template, `spec.json` and an HTTP connection. Version prompts as Git config read via `ModelConfig` and logged with the agent (Prompt Registry is Beta); promote through evaluation and roll back by redeploying. Apps: user authorization for per-user access, resources with `CAN QUERY` for least privilege.
